summary:
September 7,  

Mr. Thaon, 

You asked me one question in your letter which is rousing great forces in me: what my work will be like over the next ten years. 1 never normally think ahead, much less that far ahead. But now the question has been raised; some­ thing out of my control forces me to answer it.... so here is a third letter. I felt in February 1972 at the time I gave my Vancouver speech that some tyranny was on us, but I could not discern it clearly; I could only discern that the stilyagi would be the last to succumb to it, whatever it was. When, a few months ago, we learned about Watergate, I wrote to SF Commentary which had pub­ lished the speech: “The tyranny is so immense that we all must become teen-age rip-offs to fight it, all of us of all ages and educations and intelligences, for this tyr­ anny is that of a coup by those in power to keep power, all power, forever. This makes the nature of my future work one of great political necessity. The Nazis had a phrase for those in Gertnany who were against them but could not be detected: “Die Stille im Lande.” The silent in the land. A totalitarian state fears this sort of thing, that everybody is waving the flag and chanting “Hail the Glori­ ous leader,” but then suddenly, with neither warning nor prearranged signal, they will all toss the flags down, spit on the leader’s Cadillac, and go home, their backs turned to the symbols of authority.
